Good afternoon, Excellencies, distinguished guests, colleagues and friends. Welcome to the Secretary-General's special event on climate. I'm Melissa Fleming, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Global Communications, and it is my honor to moderate this important event. We will be opening with remarks from the Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres. Secretary-General, you have the floor.

Excellencies, dear friends, I want to thank Turkey and Australia for their efforts in the preparation of COP31. And my thanks to all the leaders and countries that are here with us today. Excellencies, the world is crying out for climate justice in mitigation, in adaptation and in finance. We must answer that call with action and we don't have a moment to lose. A super El Nino is supercharging the impacts and science tells us the world is heading for an overshoot of the 1.5 degree limit. We must make that overshoot as small and as short as possible. But emissions are still rising when they must plummet. And fossil fuel expansion continues, defying science, economics, and common sense. We have seen how fossil fuel dependence wreaks havoc, driving up costs, draining budgets, squeezing households. and leaving countries at the mercy of conflicts and decisions far beyond their borders. Meanwhile, fossil fuel companies are banking windfall profits while everyday people foot the bill. Doubling down on oil and gas will only lock in vulnerability for decades. Fortunately, we have a way out because the crisis is accelerating but so are the solutions. Renewables are the cheapest, fastest, and most secure source of new electricity almost everywhere. Clean energy has gone from alternative to unstoppable. Excellencies, in this room, We have major economies and frontline nations, energy producers and consumers, different circumstances, but a shared interest for a faster, fairer transition, for energy security and independence, and for protecting people and livelihoods. At a time of deep geopolitical division, you can show how cooperation can deliver on four fronts. First, we must accelerate. Even if fully implemented, national climate plans point to warming beyond 2 degrees. We must close that gap this decade by tripling renewables, doubling efficiency, electrifying economies, slashing methane, halting deforestation, and speeding the transition from fossil fuels. I call on every country to develop a credible roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels with clear timelines. The G20, responsible for 80% of global emissions, must lead. The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities must apply, but all countries must raise their ambition. Surging demand for power, not least from artificial intelligence, must be met with a surge in renewables, grids, and storage. Second, we must ensure fairness. A just transition must be built with affected workers and communities, creating decent jobs and strengthening social protection. Developing countries must shape it and share its benefits, starting with clean power for the hundreds of millions still without electricity, most of them in Africa. Excellences.

We must finance the transformation. The financial system must stop punishing vulnerability and start renewing climate action. That means mobilizing at least 300 billion US dollars a year for developing countries, with developed countries taking the lead. and scaling up climate finance to 1.3 trillion US dollars by 2035. Ensuring ambitious replenishment of the Green Climate Fund and the fund for responding to loss and damage. Making pollution pay, easing the burden and including repayments when disaster strikes. Easing debt burden that choked investment, that includes pausing repayments when disaster strikes. Reforming the international financial architecture to give developing countries a stronger voice and participation. Making multilateral development banks bigger, bolder, and better, and making every public dollar work harder with guarantees and other risks, risk sharing that lower the cost of capital. This allows for a lower impact. Fourth, we must protect people from the impact of climate change. Without adaptation, drought becomes hunger crises, storms become debt crises, and heat waves become killers. That is why we must triple adaptation finance. We must include resilience in every policy, in every budget, and in every infrastructure decision, and make sure that by 2027, every person on Earth is protected by an early warning system. Across all four points, we must safeguard the foundations of climate action. We must defend science and truth. We must defend the law. As the International Court of Justice has confirmed, protecting the climate is an obligation. And defending cooperation, because no country can decarbon the global economy alone or shield itself from climate chaos.

United Nations will do its part. Today, with our partners, we are launching a common platform on grids to help countries build the arteries of the clean energy age. The next phase of the Task Force on Critical Energy Transition Minerals will support six developing countries so that their mineral wealth drives local development, with added value remaining there. Since 2022, we have mobilized $2 billion for early warnings, with more than 160 countries receiving direct support to strengthen their systems. Excellencies, we must match an accelerating crisis with accelerating action, match the revolution in energy with the revolution in finance, and match rising impacts with rising protection. So I ask you all to deliver and then over-deliver. We are the first generation with the tools to end the fossil fuel age and the last who can avert climate catastrophe. Let us use them well, and I thank you.

I thank the Secretary-General for his powerful speech setting the scene and asking you all to deliver and overdeliver. It is now my pleasure to invite His Excellency, Mr. Anthony Albanese, Prime Minister of Australia, to the lectern.

Well, thank you very much to the Secretary General, colleagues. We meet at a time where temperature records are being smashed, when European communities have endured the heat waves and wildfires of an extraordinary and frightening summer. Australia knows such extreme weather events all too well. And as summer approaches, Our region is bracing for a possible record-breaking super El Nino weather pattern, with its potential for bushfires, for floods, for cyclones and storms. The dangers are indeed everywhere to see. This month, I visited Palau in the beautiful northwest Pacific, which hosted the Pacific Islands Forum. You can see for yourself there how sea level rises and changing ocean chemistry endanger the safety and economic strength so loved by the people of the world. Action is not optional. For Australia, as it must be for all of us, that action starts at home. And last year, I stood here and announced Australia's nationally determined contribution of reducing emissions by 62% to 70% by 2035. The energy transition to make this target attainable is well underway. Last summer, in the hottest quarter experienced, but also with the most energy use, in December, half of the power in our grid came from renewables, a proportion that is increasing as new renewable projects come online. And this year, of course, we have stepped up to work with Turkey to lead negotiations at COP31. To be a success, all peoples must have a voice in that vital forum. And importantly, Australia is proud to support Fiji and Tuvalu to host the pre-COP summit in the Pacific in a couple of weeks' time. Last year, with other Pacific nations, we established the Pacific Resilience Facility, the first ever Pacific-led regional climate financing mechanism. And we've backed that commitment with the contribution of $100 million towards the fund's goal of reaching $1.5 billion capitalisation. And we call upon all countries to make a contribution to these efforts on the climate frontline. It is a fact that those countries which are least responsible for the rise in emissions and the change in temperatures, such as our Pacific Island family, are those who are most affected, most affected by climate change. Where for countries such as Tuvalu and Kiribati, it is literally an existential threat. So we must act. and we must act as a matter of urgency. Australia is seeking a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for 2029-30, and if elected, we will elevate the importance of climate security, particularly in the Pacific, but more broadly as well, because we know the potential cost of inaction is too high. But we also know the benefit which is there. As the Secretary General has said, this is not only about good environmental policy, this is also good economic policy. And the truth is that it makes good macroeconomic policy to shift to a renewable led clean energy revolution. But it also is making a difference for households. And I want to conclude with this. because we need to make sure that our communities and our population go with us on the journey. And one program that we have had very successfully launched just one year ago was to match the fact that we have the highest per capita number of solar panels on roofs in the world with battery storage. And what that has resulted in, we thought 100,000 Australians would take up the subsidy to store energy so that it was useful at the peak times, at dinner time and at night. But what we found was that that target of 100,000 has not only been reached, it's been blown away with 540,000 households in a population of 28 million, so representing over a million people in just one year. What that says to me is that if we get the policy settings right, people will participate and people will engage and people will benefit because those people who have now stored energy from their roofs, of course, are taking themselves off the grid and making sure that their energy bills are reduced to zero. But also by taking that pressure off the energy grid has benefited the entire population as well as business. So we can meet this challenge. We need to argue the economic case in order to have the environmental benefit as well and the benefit for cleaner air and everything else that comes with the shift that we can and that we must do in order to protect How we have life. Thank you very much.

I thank Prime Minister Albanese, and it's my great pleasure now to welcome Michael R. Bloomberg, the United Nations Secretary-General's Special Envoy on Climate Ambition and Solutions, and also founder of Bloomberg and Bloomberg Philanthropies. Please join me in welcoming him to the stage.

Good afternoon, everyone. And let me thank the distinguished guests here today, including many heads of state. I wouldn't be misleading if I didn't say, please spend some money while you're here. Stores need the business. And thank you to the Secretary-General for bringing us all together and for his bold leadership on climate. He took office less than two months after the Paris Agreement went into effect. So I think it's fair to say he didn't have a lot of time to settle in and get comfortable. And to his great credit, he didn't waste a moment. Over the past 10 years, the world has had no more passionate advocate for action. Progress has always been as fast as it needs to be. isn't, but the world is approaching and surpassing milestones that were inevitable, unthinkable even a few years ago. Last year, more than 90% of power installation around the world was clean energy, 90%. That includes here in the United States, despite all the federal efforts to prop up fossil fuels. The US got more energy from solar power than from coal for the first time ever. Every step we've taken towards forward has saved lives by cleaning the air people breathe. The reason for this is simple. Clean energy costs have plummeted. Battery storage is rapidly improving. Solar wind and make the economic sense more than for fossil fuels for communities and for companies like Bloomberg as well. More countries recognize that clean energy is essential to their security and economic stability. At the same time, while there's still not enough climate funding going to developing countries, the amount has more than doubled since the Paris Agreement took effect. And more people are protected by early warning systems the Secretary-General has championed, which can mean the difference between life and death. Now, we all know that's not enough. Every day brings new evidence of the worsening harms of climate change. A few weeks ago, a collapsing glacier caused devastating flooding in Nepal. It has killed over 1,300 people tragically, and thousands more are still missing. Extreme heat has also caused thousands of deaths across Europe this summer. And in the United States and Canada, wildfires left more than 120 million people breathing unsafe air. The list of disasters goes on and on, and it doesn't matter where you live. No place on Earth is safe from climate change. Countries need more investment in resilient measures that protect people and in modern connected grills that will support the waves of clean energy installation. Both will require more of the kind of collaboration that has enabled progress over the past decade across government and business, philanthropy, nonprofits, and community leaders. These kinds of partnerships are behind all the work that Bloomberg and Bloomberg Philanthropies has been doing to move the world from coal to clean energy, protect the oceans, detect and fix methane leaks, help cities take action, bold action, and unlock more private funding for climate work. Working together, we can make great progress in all of these areas at COP31 and beyond. So thank you all again for your leadership and commitment and for making the time to be here. Mr. Secretary-General, we wish you all the best.
Burke, for your words and also for your great support. We will now turn to a brief scientific framing video as we wait for Prime Minister Erdogan.

We just lived through the hottest July and August on record. Global sea surface temperatures are at record high, and the worst is yet to come. Subsurface ocean temperatures are also exceptionally high. There is a huge pool of very warm ocean waters that will fuel the intensity of a very strong El Nino, maybe stronger than anything we've seen since our monitoring began. El Nino is expected to peak towards the end of 2026, but its impacts will be felt long after that, including on global temperatures. 2024 was the warmest year on record because of El Nino. We now expect that record to be broken.

So science is now clear, we will inevitably breach the 1.5 degrees Celsius limit moving into overshoot, but science is also clear that unfortunately, when we do that, We enter dangerous terrain where we're likely to cross a number of tipping point systems that not only regulate the stability of the climate system, but also fundamentally determine life support for human development.

But here's the thing, even if we do exceed 1.5 degrees, we should not forget that 1.5 degrees absolutely remains a goal. That doesn't change at all. But now we have to approach it differently. And we kind of have to come at it from above. And if we do this, well, then we can get on a overshoot peak and decline pathway. And that means keeping peak warming as low as possible, keeping the peak as short as possible, and then working back temperatures back down as quickly as possible. The future will bring many unknowns, but we know that the decisions we take now will determine if we have a chance of returning to 1.5 or below. Because every fraction of a degree avoided, every year by which overshoot is shortened, and every adaptation action taken will save lives, will protect ecosystems, and reduce economic losses.
I now invite His Excellency, Mr. Recep Tayyip Erdogan, President of the Republic of Turkey, to the lectern.

So, General Secretary.

Mr. Secretary General, Excellencies, Heads of State and Government, I extend my warmest and most respectful greetings to you all. I would like to thank the Secretary General for bringing us together today to address the issues of climate action and a just transition. As you may recall, last year here I stated that Turkey was seeking the presidency of COP31. This year we will host COP31 in Antalya province of our country from the 9th to the 20th of November. We are working to make this conference an event where the decisions we have taken on climate change are actually put into action. Together with Australia, we are conducting our preparations with an approach that will bring the expectations of different regions to the forefront. I believe that the pre-COP to be held in Fiji and the leaders gathering in Tuvalu will both help ensure that the voices of the Pacific countries are heard. Distinguished participants, the past 11 years have been the hottest period on record. The devastating floods in Nepal have painfully demonstrated that we no longer have time to lose. On this occasion, on behalf of my country and on behalf of my nation, I once again extend my heartfelt condolences and best wishes to the people of Nepal. As you know, during the first decade of the Paris Agreement, we established our common goals. Last year in Belem, we took important decisions to ensure the success of the second decade. And we must achieve much more in Antalya. We must bring ambition closer to capacity and we must bring targets closer to implementation. We have built our vision for COP31 around the concept of an implementation COP. In particular, we have set new targets on the road to 2035 in priority fields such as electrification and zero waste. and we expect your strong support for this agenda. Dear friends, any proposal that fails to reconcile our climate objectives with social and economic realities will be doomed to fail. Steps to strengthen the prosperity of countries need to be shaped in line with their own circumstances, their own capabilities, and development priorities. As inequalities in access to finance and to technology persist, It is not realistic to expect all countries to move forward all at the same pace. The stronger the link we establish between climate objectives, development and prosperity, the more effectively we can possibly make the just transition lasting and sustainable. So with these thoughts in mind, I wish our meeting every success. I extend my respectful greetings to you all with the hope of meeting with you again in Antalya.

I thank President Erdogan. And I would now like to invite our first group of leaders. From the European Union, Her Excellency Ms. Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission. From Palau, His Excellency Mr. Surangel Whipps, President of the Republic of Palau, Chair of AOSIS and Chair of PIF. And from Barbados, Honorable Mia Amor Motley, Prime Minister of Barbados and the President of the Climate Vulnerable Forum. Please come to the stage and take your places at the podiums. I see you are here. And I'm going to start with Ms. von der Leyen. The European Union has clearly recognized that the transition away from fossil fuels and energy security go hand in hand. So what steps is the European Union taking to accelerate the energy transition? And how do you plan to work with others to drive it globally?

Thank you very much, Secretary General, Prime Minister Albanese. It's good to be back in the United Nations to discuss climate and energy policy. I think the summer was a summer of truth. The recent summer months have been, as we heard from the scientists, the hottest on record, but maybe the coolest for the years to come. Europe is warming at a double the global rate, even though we account for only 6% of global emissions. Europe knows very well that the topic you're asking me to allude on, energy security, is a crucial one for us. And let me tell you the story we went through. We felt the pain of energy dependence for the first time when in 2022, Russia cut us off the gas. We had an energy dependence for gas, 45% from Russia. From one day to the next, we were cut off. We fought back. Our supplies are now more diversified. and in 2027, we will have no more Russian gas at all in the European Union. What we did, we invested massively in our homegrown clean energies, that is renewables and nuclear. We thought we are out of the woods. No way. Then came the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and we started to understand that we bitterly felt the cost of our general dependence on imported fossil fuels. You must know that the European Union does not produce any fossil fuels. So the imported fossil fuels, our dependence on that was the trigger point for the dilemma we are in. And let me give you one figure that shows how bitter this dependency is. Since the start of this conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, imported fossil fuels cost us an additional 90 billion euros without a single molecule of energy in addition. But Europe also has assets, and this is where I want to go to. There is electricity produced in Europe from homegrown renewables and nuclear. This clean electricity gives us independence, energy security, and it is affordable. Today, renewables are the world's fastest growing energy source. In Europe, 70 percent of electricity already comes from clean energies, but more has to be done, and this is my second point I want to focus on. These clean energy sources need better integration in our energy system. At the moment being, huge volumes of clean power remain unused or even wasted. Let me give you an example. Last year in the European Union, we installed more than 80 gigawatts of renewable capacity. That's good. But six times more capacity is still waiting to be connected. What a waste. So we need to boost storage and flexibility and accelerate grid connections. Our goal in the European Union is to double the share of electricity by 2040. With this, Europe could cut its fossil fuel import bill by 260 billion euros a year and invest it in the clean transition. Electrifying Europe means making Europe more independent. And allow me to conclude, what we're doing in the European Union can also be transferred to the global stage. Again, the figure from the beginning. Europe is responsible for 6% of greenhouse gas emissions, but warming twice as fast as the global rate. And therefore, of course, we get a lot of pushback also in the European Union. This is an argument that speaks for our engagement on the international scene to make sure that we have the investment in climate action that is necessary. Therefore, we are pushing forward the emission trading system worldwide, so a carbon pricing. We're pushing forward to double energy efficiency and triple renewables by 2030. And yet last year, we started the campaign together with South Africa on scaling up renewables in Africa. For all of that, we need investment. Global Gateway is our investment program of 300 billion euros for the clean transition. 150 billion euros are reserved for Africa, of which 60 billion are already invested in climate and energy, and 120 billion already programmed. So the short message I want to deliver here, we are at a watershed moment, yes, but you can count on Europe. Thank you very much.

I think Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Union. Now I would like to ask His Excellency, Mr. Serenjal Wips, President of the Republic of Palau, as chair of AOSIS and the Pacific Island Forum, you represent countries on the front lines of the climate crisis that are also showing leadership. So what action do you need to see now from the international community, and what leadership can small island developing states bring?

Excellencies, Secretary General, President Erdogan, colleagues, I was in London this summer. It was London Climate Action Week. I have to say, if you didn't believe in climate change, that was proof that it was hot and those buildings were not designed, Secretary General, to handle the heat. For us in the islands, we've been continuing to rally the call that it affects our lives every day. And really, what's most important is that every fraction of a degree matters. So first, I think it's most important that we keep within 1.5. And we do all we can to accelerate sustained emission reductions. This is not an abstract target. It's something that we need to work on diligently. And I thank the EU for taking that lead. Second, the international community must change how climate finance is mobilized and how technology and capacity to support is given out. Resources much reach the communities fully, quickly, and directly without being lost in layers of bureaucracy and adding unsustainable debt burdens. Third, we need sustained investments in regional expertise, stronger regional data systems, and local skill development. This will help SIDS develop bankable projects, implement our nationally determined goals and contributions, and build institutional capacity and retain expertise in our communities. Fourth, we must realize the ocean climate nexus, and it must be central to our climate frameworks, not treated as an afterthought. For our islands, healthy ecosystems underpin our livelihoods. Fisheries, tourism, water security, and economic stability. Climate action and ocean action must therefore advance together. Finally, Pacific and SIDS voices must be present, heard, and fully considered in decisions that affect our lives and livelihoods. A just transition cannot be designed for us. It must be shaped by us. SIDS are not just vulnerable countries seeking support. We are partners with solutions. And I just want to mention three different solutions that we are working on. One is the Unlocking Blue Pacific Prosperity Plan. And that is the program that we've committed to 100% sustainable ocean management. And on top of that, 30% protection because we believe healthy oceans go right along with a healthy planet. The oceans are our second lung. So we ask for investment in our oceans, ocean protection and sustainable ocean development. Second, the Pacific Resilience Facility. the Pacific. This is the Pacific owned facility. It's a Pacific led and Pacific centered facility to allow finance to go directly to the communities that need it most. As President Abernathy shared, I mean, Prime Minister Abernathy shared earlier. Commitments has been made. But there is more to be raised that reached the 1.5 billion dollar mark. But the scale, agility, and speed are essential for us to adapt and to mitigate escalating climate impacts. So our call, therefore, is clear. We must transition. And one of our goals in the Pacific is 100% renewable Pacific. We believe it's achievable and There is no better time than now. The Strait of Hormuz crisis has caused the cost of energy to escalate to really unsustainable levels. Fortunately, in Palau, for example, 30% of our energy is now renewable. And because of that, at least energy costs were somewhat contained. So not only for the climate, but for energy security, and economic security, we need a transition. But we need partnership, we need investments, and we need all of us working together. Our countries may be small, but the models we are building have global relevance. And we stand ready to work with all of you to deliver a just transition that leaves no country and no community behind.

Thank you, Mr. President. Prime Minister Motley, Barbados' leadership has been central to keeping the needs of climate-vulnerable countries at the heart of the international finance agenda. What are the most urgent changes needed now to tackle debt, bring down the cost of capital and unlock finance at scale? And how can some of the innovative solutions being advanced by the CBF V20 help deliver real investments for resilience and the energy transition?

Thank you very much, Secretary General, President of Turkey, Your Excellency, distinguished guests all. Thank you for this opportunity to share yet again. What are some of the needs Quite frankly, they're the same needs that we've spoken about year after year after year after year. The world has recognized that we need about $1.3 trillion by 2035 annually for developing countries. For the V20 countries, it works out to be about $490 billion a year. And to that extent, we have to understand that that amount is not easily attainable. What remains our concern is the absence of fiscal space. And I don't want to suggest that we haven't made progress because almost five years on from the Bridgetown Initiative, we saw the establishment of the Resilience and Sustainability Trust with long-term money being lent to climate-vulnerable countries for the first time with a 10 and 1/2 year moratorium. We saw the extensive use of debt swaps being utilized, debt swaps for nature, debt swaps for climate. by developing countries. We've seen as well the debt pause clauses, the natural disaster clauses that persons didn't give any chance of success and when they limited it to concessional financial institutions, they said we wouldn't get it in the marketplace. Barbados went to the market last year on the emerging market index for $500 billion million dollars and we got them with natural disaster clauses and pandemic clauses by the commercial markets in our bonds. So, these things are But we still need to go further. We still need to claim more fiscal space. There are too many countries whose high debt burden means that they cannot borrow more. And to that extent, we have to be innovative in being able to create space in a way that debt pause clauses will allow them to do. Similarly, we have to look at the cost of capital. And that is where the V20 countries have come in, have just come from the V20 forum. And in fact, in June of this year in Vienna, we signed the Vulnerability to Viability Compact, which isolates three areas: education, health, and water, water being a euphemism also for greater climate resilience. And we've agreed there with 16 international financial institutions that we will work to be able to try to create longer term lending, 40 and 50 year money we hope for, but at least 30 and 40 year money for these areas, because we cannot do the things that we need to do to build resilience with 10 and 15 year money. And we go to the annual meetings next month with a white paper to concretize these agreements that we have made. We also recognize that countries need to help themselves. and that therefore the development of individual climate prosperity plans is absolutely critical. In Barbados' case, we established an investment and resilience plan that shows our needs for investment over the course of the next decade. But we are not simply relying on external funding for that. We've made a determination, as I shared last year with you, to establish a resilience and regeneration fund locally, where every single employee in Barbados will contribute, contributes already, sorry, 0.25% of their salary without cap, matched by the employers, self-employed persons the same. And then the country use the measurement of ODA that has long eluded us in the last few years. of using 0.35% of government's GDP to put government's investment into that resilience and regeneration plan. We recognize that we need to help ourselves first while making the case for others to help us outside of this argument. What is needed? is an understanding that an unlevel playing field cannot continue. Climate-vulnerable countries pay 1.2 percentage points on average more than other countries to be able to borrow money. You cannot penalize people who are not on the front line of the crisis purely because of their vulnerability to the climate crisis. And that is what we have done by allowing this disparity in interest rates to continue. I also want to make the point that as we go forward, we are going to have to deconstruct much more of what we're doing to be able to ensure that those things that we can access are in fact available. It is one thing to say that we need finance, it is another thing to be able to access commodities and materials at affordable rates in time to be able to allow them to be executed because this is not an academic argument that we are having. So I hope that we can see that while we are making progress, there is still much room to go. And the fundamental issue comes back down to whether we can create the fiscal space, whether we can reduce the cost of capital, and whether we can so organize ourselves domestically to make projects easily executable. Thank you.

Thank you, Prime Minister, and thank you, Excellencies, for your perspectives, your commitment, and your visions. Thank you. Thank you. Please welcome Dr. Fatih Birol, who is the Executive Director of the International Energy Agency.

Mr. Secretary General, very many thanks for bringing us, all of us here today on a very important topic. Many thanks also to President Erdogan, Dr. and Prime Minister Albanese for the excellent leadership for COP31. Excellencies, today we cannot discuss any energy issue, climate issue, any economic issue, this associated from what is happening in the Middle East, the Strait of Hormuz. Some seven months ago, the most important energy artery of the world, Strait of Hormuz, is closed. And this sent shock waves to energy world and the global economy. Oil, LNG, fertilizer flows have stopped. Prices went up. Diesel prices, LPG prices, other energy prices. And many countries around the world once again understood the critical importance of energy security. And this big shock, big supply disruption, made many governments around the world reviewing, reassessing their energy strategies, their energy choices, their energy partners. As we have seen in the previous crisis, these responses are fundamental for the energy world. And, dear colleagues, I talk with many governments around the world, in Asia, in Africa, in Europe, in North America, and elsewhere. I can assure you that a big chunk, if not all, of these responses to this crisis, energy security crisis, are based on clean energy choices. Extensis, many, many years in the energy world, we had three choices in front of us. Shall I choose the most secure energy option? shall I choose the most economic energy option or shall I choose the cleanest energy option? We have to make choices, we have to make trade-offs. But when we look at the world today, for the first time since years, all of these three objectives are getting aligned, they are getting very, very close to each other. It is the reason When I look at the numbers, what is happening in the last seven months, I see a big increase in solar, wind, batteries, nuclear power, electric cars and others. And this is, I think, a very good point to note. In that context, I would like to congratulate Turkey and Australia for choosing COP31 is the main outcome, the electrification target. Today, excellencies, the share of electricity in the global energy is 23%. And based on the study of the IEA, my own institution, governments have decided to put a target. It is 35% by 2035, 35 by 35. If this target is agreed in Antalya, the beautiful city of Antalya, I can tell you it will give a very strong and unmistakable signal to the investors, finances, utilities, governments and beyond. And this in turn will not only make the world much more secure, and make the consumers being having an affordable option, but at the same time, bring the emissions down, which should be a major outcome, major good news from Antalya to the rest of the world. Thank you very much for your attention.

I thank Dr. Fatih Birol, the Executive Director of the IEA. And I would also like to thank the Secretary General and President Erdogan for their presence here for the first part of the Climate Summit 2026. They have to leave for other engagements. I would now like to invite our second group of leaders to the stage from Bangladesh, His Excellency, Mr. Tariq Rahman, Prime Minister of Bangladesh, and His Excellency, Mr. Rob Jetten, Prime Minister of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. So I'm going to ask His Excellency, Prime Minister of Bangladesh, as a climate vulnerable country, what are the key commitments of your government to addressing climate change? And what do you expect from the international community to support global climate action and to address specific vulnerabilities of countries like yours?

Thank you very much for giving me this opportunity to explain how we in Bangladesh are trying to manage this issue. Mr. Secretary-General, I thank you for convening this meeting. Ladies and gentlemen, Bangladesh contributes less than 0.5% of global greenhouse emissions. Yet it is one of the most climate-vulnerable countries. By the end of this century,

12 to 18 percent of our coastal areas could be submerged by sea level rise, affecting the livelihoods of tens of millions. Climate change has caused loss and damage equivalent to 1 percent of our GDP, and our food security is at serious risk. In this budget, two months back, we have allocated nearly 3.19 billion US dollar for climate adaption. Yet, without international support, we risk severe damage. Ladies and gentlemen, we have taken some measures to address this issue. We plan to plant 250 million trees over next five years. The reason why we want to do this, to plant 250 million trees, to bring down the heat, to bring down the temperature about one degree at least. The aim is two degree. A temporary overshoot of 1.5 degrees Celsius may not be unavoidable, but this must never become an excuse for complacency or diminished ambition. It must instead reinforce our determination in accelerating the implementation of the Paris Agreement. Our priorities are clear. This requires a rapid, just and equitable transition towards renewable energy, accelerating action on methane and other short-lived climate pollutants, and the full implementation of ambitious nationally determined contributions. Make climate finance simpler and faster, as we have heard. Help us protect our oceans and reduce the cost of financing our energy transition without pushing vulnerable countries further into debt. Jamaica, has formalized the US $36 million rural water program. And Dominica has commissioned a groundbreaking 10-megawatt geothermal plant, the first in the Eastern Caribbean. Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, my own country, we are exploring also geothermal energy. Our first attempt failed, but following Dominica's example, we are going to try again. We have also exploring wave energy and solar power. As ways of reducing even further our minimal carbon footprint. But also of ensuring energy security. We may be small island states. But we are large ocean states. The oceans support our economies. Ford security. tourism, biodiversity, and our quality of life. I wish, therefore, to conclude that the international financial architecture must be modernized to meet the 21st century realities. Resilience cannot be built on unsustainable debt and climate justice cannot remain merely an aspiration. Frontline nations must not be left to confront rising seas and mounting debt on their own. That strangles progress, limits the enjoyment of a better standard of living. I wish now to extend to my colleague from Micronesia, he says he's visited Palau and other places. I want to invite you to visit Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. We have similar concerns and similar problems. Thank you very much, God bless.

We need lives to be protected today. The time to invest in resilient cities is not tomorrow. The time is now. Thank you.

Today, I stand before you as mayor of that city and as a mother determined for a better future for all our children. As we consume more and produce faster, our convenience comes at a great cost. Forests being cleared, oceans polluted, temperatures rising. The climate crisis can feel so daunting. Thank you, panel. So I'm going to introduce the next panel. Just wait for them to be able to come. We have Lord Va'afafahi Fa'afafanua, the Prime Minister of Tonga. As a region on the front line of climate impacts, Pacific Island leaders have made Pacific Island Resilience Facility their climate investment priority. As you lead efforts towards an initial $500 million capitalization target, what steps are you taking in the region and what do you need from international partners so that this facility can deliver at the speed and scale required?

Your Excellencies, Malau'alele, on behalf of His Majesty the King to both the six and the people of the Kingdom of Tonga, I extend warm greetings from the Pacific. 10 years after the Paris Agreement, the world stands at the brink of reaching 1.5 degrees Celsius. The latest UN Environmental Program report warns that this is no longer a distant prospect, but an imminent reality. For small island developing states like Tonga, every additional fraction of a degree brings greater loss. deeper insecurity, and fewer options for survival. Across our region, stronger cyclones, rising sea levels, prolonged droughts are already placing food, water, and energy security under extreme pressure. We therefore call on the world to invest faster than climate change is changing. For Pacific nations, climate justice requires allocating finance according to vulnerability, and expediting it to those who are facing the greatest risk. Adaptation and mitigation are not competing funding choices. They are inseparable parts of effective climate response. For highly vulnerable Pacific countries, adaptation is a matter of survival. For Tonga, a just transition renewable energy is fundamental to achieving this objective. Dependence on imported fossil fuels exposes us to global shocks. Therefore, renewable energy underpins not only emissions reduction, but also our energy security and future prosperity. The transition must reflect SIDS realities, small island developing states, high costs, small markets, and limited capacity Investment must extend beyond generation to innovative technologies, resilient grids, battery energy storage systems, emergency backup systems. We're exploring geothermal power as a move to secure a more resilient energy mix. So understanding our structural reality is why accelerated investment across the climate-ocean nexus is an imperative. When the United Nations Secretary-General visited Tonga in 2024, he issued a global SOS: Save our Seas. Conservation is therefore vital to safeguarding our blue Pacific Ocean, but we must also recognize its value and responsibly harness its potential as a foundation for greater resilience and self-sufficiency. Tonga will advance this ambition by hosting the inaugural Polynesian Ocean Summit next year in May. We need genuine partnerships to scale. The climate problem requires international cooperation more than ever. In this respect, International financing systems remain too difficult to access, too slow to respond, and too distant from the communities it's intended to support. Therefore, the Pacific Resilience Facility is our response from the Pacific. PRF is the Pacific-led and Pacific-owned regional financing institution designed to deliver accessible and predictable lines financed directly. It turns our political commitments into practical action at the last mile, where climate change is already affecting homes, livelihoods, and essential infrastructure. As host of the Pacific facility, Tonga is proud to announce that more than $180 million has already been raised. Pacific Island Forum leaders are committed to working with our partners to reach the initial capitalization target of $500 million by COP31. Prime Minister of Tonga. And I would now like to turn to the Third Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Ecological Transition of Spain. Thank you. Thank you very much. Good afternoon to everyone. For me, it's really a great pleasure to be delivering what is our policy, our message from Spain today in this very important summit. I will deliver my speech in Spanish. So, olas de calor.

Extreme heat waves, record unprecedented temperatures in our oceans and in our Mediterranean Sea. Floods are covering More than, and more than 300,000 hectares affected by the fires, all of this in my country in less than 12 months in my country.

This is an energy system that is not only more sustainable but also more affordable and of course more autonomous. And something that we take very seriously in Spain is that we have harnessed the power of civil society to do all of this. This is something that we put forward, something that we put forward as Spain was the debt for sustainable swaps and also pursuing global fiscal justice and more inclusive governance. And I'll conclude now. I think that we stand at a crucial turning point now, where we need to build bridges, we need to work together, be more ambitious than ever. And today, we think that here today, we need to breathe ambition. And one message I think it's important for all of society is that many more of us are convinced than are not convinced by this. So this roadmap isn't an option, it is the option. because it makes sense. Thank you.

So let's see. I would now like to turn to the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Maldives. The Maldives have long been a leading voice for small island developing states and calling for adaptation to be prioritized. Greetings from the Maldives, the sunny side of life. Thank you, moderator. Ladies and gentlemen, excellencies, I would like to put it very simply. Three things must change. First, We must close the gap between finance promised and finance delivered for adaptation. Developed countries must meet their existing obligations and deliver the commitments already made through the COP process. There's no substitute for that. Private, blended, and innovative finance can add to public finance. They cannot replace it. And for SIDS, finance must be predictable, accessible, and largely grant-based or highly concessional. Protecting people from climate change should not push countries deeper into debt. Second, we need to move from financing projects to financing resilience. In the Maldives, adaptation means protecting our islands and shorelines, making critical infrastructure stronger, protecting our coral reefs, safeguarding communities and livelihoods. That means resilience must be built into development itself, and finance must reach countries faster. should not spend years navigating complex process to access finance. Third, we must judge adaptation by results on the ground. Let us ask ourselves, are communities safe? is infrastructure stronger? Are livelihoods more secure? Are countries better able to withstand the next shock? That should be the measure of success, not simply how much was pledged or how many projects were approved. And one final point, adaptation is not a substitute for mitigation. There are limits to what any island can adapt to. The more we delay cutting emissions, the harder and more costly adaptation becomes. So at COP31, let us move adaptation from planning to protection. I thank you. Thank you very much.

I would now like to turn to the Right Honourable Ed Miliband, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, United Kingdom. Mr. Miliband has made significant progress in its domestic energy transition. whilst being an important provider of climate finance to developing countries. So what further actions will you take to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels at home and internationally to scale up climate finance and also mobilize investments for developing countries?

Well, thank you so much, and it's great to be here. I want to thank the Secretary General for his incredible work on these issues over the last decade. And I also want to say what a pleasure it is to be here with the incoming COP31 presidency, and we look forward to success in Turkey later on this year. Let me make three points to answer your question. The first is about domestic action. I think it's really important to frame domestic action in the right way. This is about the climate crisis and environmental care, but it is about much more than that. It's about energy security, it's about jobs, and it is also about national security too. I hosted an event earlier today with foreign ministers from a range of countries talking about the national security threats we face from climate. In terms of what we are doing domestically within that context, we've had the largest offshore wind auction in the history of Europe. We've got record solar power, record wind power. We're seeing investment in warm homes. We've legislated for a target of 87% reduction in emissions by 2040. We've banned new licenses to explore new oil and gas fields, all within that context of this big argument about how do we get energy security, how do we create the jobs of the future, and how do we do the right things for future generations, and we will push on further, including on the transition away from fossil fuels. Second point, I want to say something about our international responsibilities, and I think it's really important to say that international responsibilities are being fulfilled, yes, because of the demands of justice, yes, because of the demands of international solidarity, but also, frankly, self-interest. Unless we all tackle this problem together, then we are all going to suffer separately from the climate crisis, even more than we are suffering already. To that end, we've been delighted to pledge to the new TFFF, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, of 400 million pounds, which is an innovation, a great innovation from the COP30 presidency in Brazil. Today, we're announcing an investment of 330 million pounds in the Global Environment Facility, which is a very, very important project, as well as other additional public finance. The broader point I would make, though, and I'm going to be at the annual meetings later on next month in Bangkok is we need more MDB reform to help countries to access finance. Because the points that our colleague from the Maldives made about not just quantity of finance, but quality of finance, access to finance, the balance between grants and loans, the financing of adaptation, these are all incredibly important arguments. And actually, let's be frank, the reform of the international financial system is very, very much a work in progress to meet the demands of climate resilience. The last point I just want to make is a sort of point of optimism, because it's so easy to be pessimistic at these events. The people who want to undermine the project we are talking about and what we are talking about, there are the deniers, there are the delayers who say this problem doesn't exist, there are the delayers People who say, let's do it, but not yet. But then there are also the defeatists. And the defeatists, I think, actually are now a bigger problem than the deniers and the delayers. They're the people who say, well, you've been trying to do this for 30 years, 40 years, and nothing's changed. And so there's no point in even trying. Now, I think it's up to us to tell all the defeatists that they are wrong. Because I actually think this is a shining example of the success of multilateralism. When I left the not very successful Copenhagen Summit 2009, we were heading for a four degree or more world of global warming. Today we're heading for something like a two and a half degree world. Now that's very bad, don't get me wrong, but it is multilateralism, it is countries working together to tackle this problem that has produced the gains that we have. So I think it's very, very important in this context to talk about what we need to do further talk about how we need to act internationally, but also to make this argument that actually multilateralism works. And at a time when it is more under question than it has been for generations, I actually think that the climate efforts that we are making together and the will that I see from countries across the world to tackle this problem should give us confidence and optimism about the future. Thank you so much.

Secretary of State Miliband, and also for giving us that injection of optimism about multilateralism. I'd now like to turn to His Excellency Mr. Karsten Schneider, Federal Minister of the Environment. He has a very long title. I'll say it again.
Yeah.

Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation, and Nuclear Safety. Germany is playing a pivotal role in both the energy transition and global climate finance. So what concrete steps are you taking to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels, also while scaling up affordable finance for developing countries?

Yeah, thanks. Thanks a lot for the question. And I fully agree with my honorable minister colleague from the United Kingdom towards the question of multilateralism. and that these, not only the big debates, but the decisions that were made at COPs, as under the Lago and from Brazil, thanks a lot for that COP, and we are looking forward to the new presidency in Turkey, that this delivers. And I will be concrete. Germany today, the German government, in my absence, but I prepared the proposal, we published national roadmap for and decided about it, a national roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels. This was one of the debating points, you know that. And now we took up the debate and decided. As an industrial, as the third biggest industrial country in the world, and there are some deniers in Germany, but we show that we can make it. What is in? Germany has committed by law to becoming climate neutral by 2045. This is just 19 years. This requires systematically phasing out fossil fuels in all sectors. The share of renewable energy in electricity production is growing rapidly, particularly of wind and solar power. It already accounts for around 55% of of Germany's gross electricity consumption and is projected to rise at least to 80% by 2030. Last week in Hamburg, I opened the offshore wind park, 1 gigawatt. 10 years, okay, was too long, but 1 gigawatt and no public funding, private finance. And all the energy is sold for the next years. It works. Together, with the phase out of coal no later than 2038, probably it will be earlier, the decarbonization of the special power plants and the expansion of the electricity grids, this will enable us to achieve a climate-neutral electricity supply. The electrification of energy consumption is also gaining ground. For instance, heat pumps and district heating are replacing oil and gas-based heating systems. 2025 saw more heat pumps sold for the first time in Germany than gas-based heating systems. The ramp-up of electric mobility is gaining momentum in Germany. In August 2026, battery electric passenger cars accounted for over 32% of of newly registered vehicles. And there are another 15% hybrid. So it's close to 50% of all everything. The industry where electrification is economically viable, it should be consistently harnessed. That's where it should be systematically developed. This will enable Germany to significantly reduce imports of fossil fuels and lower its dependence on supply chains vulnerable to geopolitical crisis. The 2026 Climate Action Program presented in March has a total of 67 measures. It will ensure savings of almost 7 billion cubic meters of natural gas and some 4 billion liters of petrol by 2030. We call on all countries worldwide to also accelerate the energy transition. This is the only way we can keep the 1.5 degree target within reach together. At international level, Germany supports the COP 31's presidency's focus on electrification. Good proposal. This is because electrification and transition away from fossil fuels goes hand in hand. To gain broad agreement on a future global electrification target, we must start forging an international alliance with the global south now. COP31 should also deliver an ambitious electrification package with specific implementation steps. The global Electrify Now initiative can play an important role in these efforts. And at the same time, it is important to ensure that transitioning away from fossil fuels remains high on the international agenda. So Germany supports, as I mentioned, the roadmap process of Brazil's COP 30 presidency. We encourage the COP 31 and COP 32 presidencies to continue this process. Now to the international climate finance. As a committed partner, Germany supports developing countries in transitioning away from fossil fuels and strengthening their resilience. this end, we provided and mobilized a total of 1.8 billion euros for international climate finance in 2024. We are also committed to improving the overall framework to set the clear course for investment. This will mobilize more financial resources for transitioning away from fossil fuels and not only Maldives, but all the other countries. You can count on Germany. We stand ready to work with partners from all countries and sectors, and we want to enable countries to chart their own course to energy security and prosperity. Thank you.

This distinguished panel for your very powerful statements. Thank you very much. Thank you. Please welcome now Mr. Pascal Donohue, Managing Director and Chief Knowledge Officer of the World Bank Group.

Creating jobs, improving lives, while building economies that are resilient, efficient, competitively, fiscally sound, and built to last. And in that fiscal year, we delivered $48 billion in climate co-benefits from our own balance sheets. Put all of this together, this is $96 billion of support. But the message from all of this, for all of you is very, very clear that public finance alone will not be enough. Governments, multilateral development banks, we must work together to reduce risk, to strengthen policy, and to build more projects so that private capital can move at scale. So we have so much to do. The World Bank Group stands ready to be your implementation partner, the partner that countries need to bring together financing, analytics, guarantees and private capital to turn plans into results. We need your support to implement your national climate plans, to remove barriers to private investment and to match ambition with finance so that we can deliver at scale against this great challenge. And this is how climate smart development can turn ambition into investment to partner with you to deliver impacts and results for those that we serve at scale. Thank you.

Thank you very much to the Managing Director and Chief Knowledge Officer of the World Bank Group, Mr. Pascal Donohue. And I'd now like to introduce the next group of leaders and ask them to come to the stage. We have His Excellency, Mr. Kalani Kaneko, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade of the Republic of the Marshall Islands. The Honorable D. Ramphal, Minister of Foreign Affairs, Regional Integration and International Trade of Mauritius. His Excellency, Mr. Jamhur Hidayat, Minister of Environment of Indonesia. His Excellency, Mr. Mohammad Ali Nafti, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Indonesia. And His Excellency Maxim Vladimirovich Rihinshkov, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Belarus. So I'm going to start with the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade of the Republic of the Marshall Islands, sir. As the world enters an era, 1.5 degrees overshoot, the consequences will fall hardest on countries like the Marshall Islands. What does adaptation look like from your perspective and what must be done to ensure that the world supports you in your work while accelerating efforts to bring the temperatures back under 1.5 degrees?

Thank you for the great question, Assistant Secretary General, Excellencies. First, allow me to convey sincere apology on behalf of Madam President and Heine. She had very much hope to be here today, but is unfortunately unwell. Let me share with you an example of what adaptation looked like in the Marshall Islands. We have just completed a new seawall It will protect thousands of lives, thousands of people. But the story behind the seawall is telling. It took 10 years, eight years to plan and two years to find financing and to build. Eight years to plan and find financing and two years to build. total of 10 years. And this is the only one of many islands in my country. We do not have this kind of time. Sea walls, resilient agriculture, and health systems. These things are crucial. But they are totally insufficient in the face of unchecked fossil fuels. 1.5 to stay alive has been a rallying cry for small island states and the High Ambition Coalition, which my country convenes with good reasons. Once we go above 1.5, many measures to adapt just won't be feasible, and the loss and damage will be devastating. So the first step in adapting to an era of overshooting or overshoot is by limiting that overshoot. The Pacific has committed to a regional energy strategy to make our region fossil fuel free. Every region should have a roadmap that figures out what barriers are to this transition and all they can turn or torn down. And the next step is money. Our national adaptation plan will cost billions to implement. This is well beyond what our economy can support. Those who think that we can depend on private sector have never experienced the realities of a small island developing state's economy. For us, adaptation depends on grant-based or highly concessional finance that comes quickly and without a million string attached. This should not be impossible. Simplifying procedures, speed up disruptions, put the money in the reach of those of us that need it the most. In the Marshall Islands, we have established the Marshall Islands Resilient and Adaptation Trust Fund, the MIRAT, a one-stop shop for donors to support adaptation and resilience building, led by and for the Marshallese people. I invite donors, let us show how we can make even the most vulnerable countries resilient. But even if we adapt, loss and damage is unavoidable. We see it in the devastation that makes headlines and in insidious changes, the migration of tuna, the king tides that eats away our shores, coral bleaching, The answer must be swift and full restitution. This is the only path to justice in context of an overshoot we did not cause and have the fewest resources to respond to. Assistant Secretary-General, thank you for your extraordinary climate leadership. We must all follow your lead. We must end our dependency on fossil fuels. And we support the communities that are preparing for and dealing with the carnage those fossil fuels have already caused. Thank you.

And I am now pleased to ask the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Honorable D. Ramphal. of Mauritius. Mauritius combines the perspective of a small island developing state with the experience as a regional financial center. How can public and private finance be brought together to scale investment in resilience? And what support is needed from international partners?

Thank you. Let me, first of all, thank the Secretary-General for having convened this important meeting on climate action. There are two parts to this question. One is about setting the right mechanism in our financial sector in order to mobilize private and public finance. And the second part of the question is about getting the support of international partners. I have to say that in this task, it has not been easy for Mauritius. It was a difficult task because we have unfortunately had to pay for the success of, for our own economic success. Well, first of all, according to the latest world report, for us to support our coast, improve water security, and also to support our transition to clean energy, and we need approximately 5.6 billion USD for the next 25 years to fund climate adaptation and green energy initiatives. Now, this is impossible for a small country like Mauritius. And secondly, we are not eligible for concessional finance given our GDP per capita. So luckily, we managed to use our dynamic financial sector as a conduit for private investment into bankable projects that are related to resilience and adaptation. Now, we also shifted our approach from a public led expenditure to a strategy where public capital acts as a catalyst to unlock private investment. So we are trying to pioneer scalable, replicable models of blended finance. We have been working on four strategic pillars for mobilising private sector finance. Firstly, sovereign de-risking mechanism. Secondly, institutional asset activation. Thirdly, sustainable capital markets. And lastly, the modernized public-private partnerships. Now, unlocking these capital flows requires a strong national ecosystem that turns high-level climate commitments into transparent, actionable, market mechanism. So, Mauritius is strengthening this ecosystem by developing comprehensive frameworks, including its national green taxonomy and robust climate change reporting guidelines, with the support of international partners. And secondly, we have embedded climate resilience metrics into the procurement and design stages of public private partnerships Mauritius can help ensure that private concessionaires build and manage public infrastructure able to withstand growing environmental risk while setting a model for sustainable long-term asset management. Now, the second part of the question about the need of support from international partners. Let me say this from the outset. One thing is very clear. Global partners must move beyond outdated aid models to highly concessional financing, long-term credit enhancements, and targeted grants that help absorb the high upfront cost of adaptation. Through international grants, concessional loans, targeted subsidies, blended finance structures, first loss guarantees, and strong public-private partnerships. Small island developing states like Mauritius can improve the risk return profile for private investors. Now, this approach can turn capital-intensive adaptation projects in coastal protection, renewable energy, and climate-smart agriculture from high risk obligations into stable, commercially viable and bankable assets for institutional investors. Our ability and that of all SIDS to deliver this model at speed and scale depends, of course, on predictable and enhanced support from the international community and multilateral financial institutions. Now, before I end, allow me just to give a few examples on how public and private finance are mobilized to fund climate president related projects. First, we created a climate and sustainability fund using a corporate levy and a dedicated national fund. Secondly, we came with the home solar project for individual household. And this shows blended concessional finance in practice. International concessional resources covers half the project cost while the public utility will finance the rest. Therefore, households receive the resulting benefits without bearing the upfront capital cost. Third, we have the Mauritius Renewable Energy Investment Facility, which attracts independent power producers and international investors through streamlined approvals, fiscal incentives, sovereign guarantees, blended finance tools, and a pipeline of bankable projects. Therefore, to conclude, Mauritius, as an established international financial centre with a sound regulatory framework, stands ready to host entities involved in nature and climate entities. We can provide a reliable platform for issues and trading for such activities. Thank you.

I would now like to ask the Minister of Environment for Indonesia, His Excellency Mr. Jamhar Hidayat. your work, your government has started to work towards a massive 100 gigawatt expansion of renewable energy. Thank you, Madam Rata. Thank you, Chairs, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. The Paris Agreement provides our compass. Yet as the window to keep 1.5 degrees Celsius within this rapidly narrows, our task is to bridge the gap between global commitments and tangible results, guided by equity and common but differentiated responsibility and respective capabilities. Under the leadership of President Prabowo Subianto, Indonesia is translating climate ambition into concrete action through our enhanced NDC, Nationally Determined Contribution, and second NDC, charting a pathway toward net zero emissions by 2060 or sooner. For us, climate action must go hand in hand with economic growth, energy security, poverty eradication, and resilience. Our development paradigm is clear. Growth and environmental protection must advance together. To keep 1.5 degree Celsius within reach, Indonesia is accelerating economy-wide action. We are advancing our net zero 2030, reducing emissions from waste and methane, and transforming our industrial sector through two complementary tracks, decarbonizing existing industries and designing new low-carbon industry from the outset. Now, Indonesia constructing the huge plants of electric vehicles that can share within the 300 million population. This transformation will be supported by innovation and responsible deployment of carbon capture, utilization, and storage, drawing on Indonesia's geological formation and growing technological capability. In the energy sector, we are rolling out an ambitious 100 gigawatts solar program within the next three years and directing 70% of new national power capacity. 12S, we also exploring the potencies of our geothermal energy. We are also strengthening energy security through the nationwide implementation of B50 biodiesel. Our transition must be just, orderly, country-led and people-centered, strengthening energy security and affordability, creating decent green jobs and local value, as well as protecting vulnerable communities. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, while Indonesia is mobilizing domestic resources and developing carbon market instruments, Climate finance must be affordable, accessible and predictable and commensurate with the scale of the challenge through national endeavor and international support. We must also scale up support for responding to loss and damage. Vulnerable developing countries need timely, adequate and accessible resources to address the economic and non-economic impact of extreme weather events and slow onset climate change. Adaptation must advance alongside mitigation. As an archipelagic nation, Indonesia is advancing the giant sea wall along Java's northern coast while protecting and restoring mangrove and other coastal ecosystems to safeguard communities, livelihood, and development. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, as we look ahead to COP31 in Antalya, we must demonstrate credible progress in implementing and scaling up the new collective quantified goal. Antalya must also prove that multilateralism can deliver for those most vulnerable to the climate crisis. Indonesia stands ready to deepen partnership that turn climate ambition into genuine development, opportunity, and resilience for all. I thank you.

Thank you, Your Excellency. And I would now like to turn to the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Tunisia. What is Tunisia doing to accelerate the shift towards clean energy and build resilience to climate impacts? And what support do you need from international partners?

Thank you, Madam Moderator. Many thanks. Let me first underline that Tunisia is firmly committed to accelerating the transition towards a low-carbon and climate-resilient development model. while ensuring that climate action supports our development priorities. Indeed, our new national determined contribution 3.0 reflects a significant increase in our climate ambition as we are aiming at reducing our carbon intensity by 62% by 2035 compared with 2012. 2010 levels with half of the ambition of this ambition condition on enhanced international support. Of course, energy is indeed at the heart of this transformation. We are working to improve energy efficiency and reduce our dependence on fossil fuels as we are accelerating the deployment of renewable energy with the objective of reaching 35% renewable energy in our electricity mix by 2030. At the same time, we are strengthening resilience to climate impacts, particularly in water security, agriculture, food systems, and coastal areas, especially in light of the sea water raise threat. Our ambition needs to be matched by the means to fulfill it. Implementing our NDC will certainly need no less than $50 billion. This is why Tunisia is also strengthening its capacity to mobilize climate finance. in this vein, on October 7th, in partnership with UNDP, we will convene a national workshop in the International Diplomatic Academy in Tunisia, aiming at facilitating the access to multilateral climate finance, bringing together national stakeholders and development partners to identify practical ways to better mobilize and channel climate finance towards NDC 3.0 priorities. Yet, national efforts alone cannot meet the scale of the challenge. Excellencies, we need our international partners to provide greater access to concessional finance and grants, technology transfer, capacity building, and stronger investment partnerships, particularly for renewable energy and adaptation programs. We also need a financial architecture that is more accessible, predictable, suitable, and responsive to the needs of developing and climate-vulnerable countries. Tunisia is committed, ladies and gentlemen, to assume its charge. What we need is a stronger commitment from our partners to turn climate ambition into investment in concrete actions and climate actions into resilience, sustainable growth, and shared prosperity. I thank you so much.

Lindsay, and now I'd like to ask the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Belarus, what steps will Belarus take to accelerate the shift towards clean energy and what international cooperation is needed for a just and orderly transition?

Thank you, dear Madam Moderator. I would just like to say a few words as to how we characterize the situation that we're in today. Everybody says that climate change represents the greatest challenge of our time. Indeed, we are continuing to see alarming trends in this area, more frequent droughts, forest fires, the drying up of rivers. We see this not only in vulnerable regions of the planet, but also in the center of Europe, which has now become a vulnerable place. And we do need to ask honestly, who created this crisis? The industrial might of the West was built on coal and steel for centuries, first their own, and then through the plunder of colonial countries. It was when the extensive development model exhausted itself, when that happened, Some countries began to manipulate the green agenda and try to curb the development of resource-rich countries of the global majority. And this policy that is completely hypocritical is really accompanied by actions that worsen the situation on our planet. For example, the unfurling of armed conflicts that have a colossal environmental footprint from oil spills and explosions to emissions from military equipment and fires at oil storage facilities. Second, through illegal unilateral sanctions. These impede dozens of countries having access to clean technologies and renewable energy. Thirdly, through boycotting the airspace, for example, of Belarus and Russia, it is making it much more difficult for many countries to travel. It's lengthening routes and therefore increasing planes' carbon footprints. Fourth, through the politicisation of environmental platforms, they're becoming less engaged in addressing real problems and rather are turning into instruments of pressure. If we stop doing this, then it would all be better for our planet. Belarus, nonetheless, is acting. We pay particular focus on our transition to clean energy. We have decreased greenhouse gases by 40% as compared to the 1990s. So over a 36-year period, we've decreased it by 40%. We have a national climate change adaptation plan to 2040. This document sets out systemic measures to protect water resources, to introduce drought-resistant technologies in agriculture and to reduce risk for all sectors of the economy. We are also effectively developing green and nuclear energy. We have a Belarusian nuclear power plant now commissioned that has allowed for an annual reduction of greenhouse gas emissions by more than 7 million tonnes. This is a real contribution to protecting the climate. So we have also had a positive effect of electrifying our public transport system and our railways, and we have a whole project there. Madam moderator, the climate crisis can only be overcome together. We would call upon everyone to work together without double standards to preserve the planet for future generations.
