Mohamed, Africa has contributed little to the climate crisis while facing some of its most severe consequences. Where do you see the greatest opportunity for African climate leadership, and what do you need to see from others internationally?

Thank you. Firstly, thank you to the UN Secretary-General and to the Climate Action Team for convening us. This is precisely the moment when the UN needs to speak loudly and clearly. Excellencies and distinguished delegates, the climate crisis has not become less dangerous because the politics have become challenging. And so it's great to have a UN Secretary-General prepared to use the authority of the office to confront the climate crisis at a time when governments and powerful, enforcing foreign interests are taking us in the wrong direction. And so for that, I must say thank you to the UN Secretary-General. Excellencies and distinguished guests, We've heard the world is running out of time on climate change. At the same time, Africa is facing a huge development challenge as millions of its people still lack access to reliable access to electricity. Its young population needs jobs, and its countries need faster economic growth. The good thing is Africa can help meet both challenges. We have extraordinary renewable resources. Africa has 60% of the world's best solar resources, yet it receives only around 2% of the global clean energy investment. That is an extraordinary mismatch between opportunity and investment. Africa needs to be recognized. not simply as a continent on the frontline of the climate crisis, but as a place where its solutions can be built at scale. The opportunity is enormous and the window to seize it is now. Across the continent, we're already seeing an energy transformation beginning from the ground up. Solar is becoming cheaper and more accessible. Countries have an enormous potential in wind, geothermal, and other renewables. Renewables are now the cheapest and the fastest source of new power, creating opportunities to expand electricity access, support businesses, create jobs, and drive economic growth. But the opportunity goes much further than generating clean electricity. Africa needs to use clean, affordable energy to industrialize. We need to power factories, process our own resources, manufacture goods, build new green industries, and create jobs for a growing population. That is what African climate leadership should mean, as it uses the transition to a low-carbon economy to accelerate development and raise the standards of living. But we cannot repeat a model in which Africa exports raw materials and imports finished products. The energy transition should help African countries capture more value from their resources and build competitive industries at home. But that requires investment at a scale that Africa cannot provide on its own. But Africa cannot do this with one hand tied behind its back. As the Secretary-General made clear yesterday, we need reform of the international financial system. You need effective debt relief and action to stop illicit financial flows, draining resources from developing countries. These issues are directly connected to the climate transition. The international community needs to tackle the cost of capital. We've had this a number of times. That is a scandal of justice, injustice in this process. We need to tackle an unfair financial architecture that makes it far more expensive to build renewable energy in Africa than in richer countries. And African countries together with vulnerable countries can help build global cooperation frameworks and mechanisms needed to change this and deliver just transition that is orderly, fair and financed for people in developing countries such as the proposed fossil fuel treaty and the transition away from fossil fuels. Roadmap that has been developed. If the world wants to Africa to accelerate its clean energy transition, then the financial system has to make that possible and mechanisms of cooperation have to change. And friends, climate justice also means finance for adaptation and loss and damage for countries already suffering impacts they did almost nothing to cause. Africa should have the resources to protect communities, strengthen infrastructure and build economies that can withstand these impacts. In conclusion, Excellencies, my message is, Africa is not asking the world to come and rescue it. We are asking the world to stop putting obstacles in the way of Africa building the clean energy future that the whole world needs. We want to turn our renewable energy resources into reliable electricity. We want to use that electricity to power industries, create jobs, and build businesses. We want African countries to manufacture more of what they currently import and capture more value from the resources they already possess. And we want to do that while helping the world meet its climate goals. Africa does not lack climate ambition, sunlight, or solutions. What it lacks is a fair financial system that allows us to turn those advantages into prosperity. And let's together make that happen. Thank you.

Thank you, Mohammed, for highlighting Africa's leadership and need for climate justice. I'll now turn to Anne Yellema, the executive director of 350.org. Anne, civil society movements have called for climate justice and accountability and helped put climate right at the top of leaders' agendas. At this stage of the climate crisis, where can citizen movements exert the greatest pressure for the fastest action?

Thank you. Your Excellency, distinguished guests, we have heard many times today that the question is no longer whether we should end our addiction to fossil fuels, or even if we can. The challenge now is to do it fast enough to stem the tide of destruction and death while we still can, and to do it in a just and equitable way that creates opportunity and prosperity for everyone, as Muhammad has so powerfully outlined. This demands vision and courage from national and local leaders, but it also needs countries to move together. Yet, since as civil society, our job is to speak frankly, let me name the elephant that is still hiding in this room, despite the fact that there are very few other people left in the room. International cooperation on climate has become as gridlocked and fractious as the streets of Manhattan outside this building today, despite the tireless efforts of Secretary General Guterres, ASG Hart, and many others in this room and outside of this room. In this situation, I think that there are two things that civil society can move forward in this moment that will help to break the impasse and strengthen the hands of our elected leaders to take bolder action. First, citizens must hold fossil fuel companies to account and demand that governments make polluters pay. It is not right that these companies keep pocketing enormous sums, $25 billion a day, every day, for the past half a century. while leaving the public to pay for the harms that they have known full well that they are causing. As so many speakers today have told us, climate disasters and mounting costs of adaptation are pushing many governments deep into debt distress, forcing cuts to vital public services and sustainable development goals, and driving families, women in particular, into poverty and hunger. Taxing the excess profits of the fossil fuel industry is the fairest way to raise the public funds needed to address these increasingly urgent financial challenges, while also fixing the broken system that incentivizes fossil fuel companies to keep expanding production by allowing them to privatize vast gains while socializing even greater harms. Second, it is time to demand affordable clean energy as a right for all and not as a privilege. Burning endless amounts of scarce, globally traded commodities is actually ludicrously, exorbitantly expensive as a way to power your economy. And that's why many governments spend a big chunk of their budgets on subsidies to try to make energy cheaper for consumers and businesses. But even with those trillions in taxpayer subsidies going to fossil energy every year, the fossil-based energy system, according to research by the Rockefeller Foundation, has left almost 4 billion people unable to access or afford enough power to lift themselves and their communities out of poverty. So citizens should demand that governments support and scale up bottom-up renewable energy revolution that Mohammed spoke about by supporting, by shifting those subsidies, those fossil fuel subsidies to 100% renewable solutions that will provide abundant, reliable energy to all regardless of income and make energy poverty a thing of the past, creating health and wealth for all. In a situation like we are today, we For every fraction of a degree matters. So too, every voice is needed. In times as politically challenging as these, citizens' demands for accountability and their hopes for a better and safer future are the most powerful lever that we have. Thank you.

Thank you, and for your continued advocacy. Thank you. I'll now turn to Hindou Ibrahim. advocate, SDG advocate and president of the Association of Indigenous Women and Peoples of Chad. Hindu, indigenous peoples hold generations of knowledge about protecting ecosystems and adapting to changing environments. What more needs to be done to move beyond consulting indigenous communities and instead recognizing them as leaders and decision makers?

Thank you, moderator. Firstly, may I request everyone please congratulate, applaud the SD, the DSD, and all the climate team by putting people in the planet in the center of all their decision, please. Then I would like to thank everyone in this room that is paid to listen the voice of people. When we speak about climate in room like this, we often speak in numbers, 1.5 degrees, billions of dollars, ton of emissions, and disease. But I come from a community where climate change is not a number. It is whether there is water for our cattles, whether there is pastures tomorrow, or whether a family can remain on the land where their ancestors have lived for generations. I am a Bororo indigenous from Chad, and my grandmother taught me something very simple when I was a child. Listen to the land, listen to the wind. Listen to the rain, to the insect, to the plant, to the animals. They tell you when you need to move. They tell you when something is wrong. For generations, this knowledge has helped our people to adapt and to survive. This was a simple tradition for some. But it was a climate knowledge. It was a natural technology that do not need electricity. And today, Indigenous peoples hold enormous knowledge about ecosystem, resilience, adaptation. But too often, we are invited in the climate discussion to tell our history, while someone else make the decision about us. And I think we need to change the cautions. We should stop asking, how can we better consult Indigenous peoples? And start asking, how can we share decision-making power with Indigenous peoples? Because consultation without power can become simply listening without changing anything. We are right holders. We are knowledge holders. We are living with the ecosystem and solution makers. And we are not just a beneficiary waiting for someone to bring us solutions. We are already building solutions in our communities. So power without resources is not enough. We cannot ask indigenous peoples to protect forests, restore land, and adapt to climate change while the money is staying in capital, institutions, and system that rarely reach the communities that do the work. If we trust communities with the responsibility of protecting our ecosystem, we must trust them with the resources to do it. And as we accelerated the gas transition, we must be careful. We are moving away from fossil fuel. We are building renewable energy. We need critical minerals. We are expanding conservation. But every time we make this decision, we should ask three simple questions. Whose land, whose resources, this decision because we cannot build a green future using the same patterns of exclusion and extraction that create this crisis. A transition is not truly just if people are displaced from their homeland without consent. So I will finish there. where I began, with my grandmother. She taught me to listen to land. Today, the land is speaking loudly. Communities in Nepal, in the Sahel, in the Pacific are the first victims. Listen to the land, to the people, and please answer the land. And then give indigenous peoples their power and their resource, and we will act. I thank you.

Thank you, Hindou, for so powerfully and passionately bringing

the leadership of indigenous peoples the meeting. I will now move on to our final speaker on the civil society panel, Omar Faruq, the General Secretary of the Federation of Somali Trade Unions. Omar, the climate transition will ultimately succeed or fail in people's workplaces and communities. What does a genuinely just transition look like for workers, particularly workers in countries already facing economic and climate pressures?

Thank you, moderator, excellencies, distinguished guests. I would like to thank the UN Secretary-General and his excellent climate team for convening this important climate summit and for bringing member states and key stakeholders, including trade unions and civil society, into these global discussions. Speaking for the global trade union movement, who represent the working masses across the continent and of the ages of the International Trade Union Confederation, a genuinely just transition means that workers, their families and their communities must not pay the price for climate-induced crisis that they did not create. For workers in countries facing poverty, debt, unemployment, conflict, and repeated climate disasters, transition cannot mean losing today's jobs and livelihoods for uncertain promises of future green jobs. It must deliver decent work, labor rights, social protection, skills and safe workplaces. It must also protect women, young people, migrant workers, and the millions of workers in the informal economy that we see day in, day out. Developing countries must receive adequate climate financing, as my colleague is talking about, through grantees, not additional debt burdens. Workers and their trade unionists must have a formal seat and a real voice at the table because they represent the working people. These are the working masses. People-centered climate policies and actions must be shaped through genuine social dialogue, not imposed from above. In other words, we must democratize the discussions and the decisions that we make about climate change and climate action. One point must not be overlooked. A just transition cannot be used as an excuse to delay climate action. Governments must act must cut emissions and move away from fossil fuels fairly while investing in climate-resilient communities and decent green jobs. My country, Somalia, offers a practical example. Through sustained campaigning and social dialogue, we as a trade union movement helped enshrine just transition principles in law, a first for Africa. We also secured their inclusion in our national developmental architecture that we call National Transformation Plan, in our NDC 3.3 as well. If Somalia can take these steps despite enormous economic and climate pressures, other countries can do the same. This commitment must now be fully and judiciously implemented. The other very important point that civil society and organized labor movement can play role is preserving information integrity. Information integrity is very essential. We must protect it so that workers, communities, and the wider world are not misled about the causes of climate change. The solution is required or who should pay the cost. People need accurate information about climate risks, financing, technologies, and how climate policies will affect their lives. Excellencies, disinformation and misinformation create fear, divide communities, and weaken public trust. Journalists are essential to preserving information integrity and holding decision makers accountable. In other words, information integrity is the antidote to climate disinformation. And as a journalist myself, safety of journalists is also very paramount. Several climate reporting journalists or environmental journalists have paid very dear price. They were victimized and targeted because they unearthed uncomfortable truth. They have been the voice of the citizen is they have told the truth that all of us need to hear, but they have paid the ultimate price. So the safety and security of journalists is also very important. I conclude just transition must protect rights. Those rights are human and labor rights, reduce inequality and deliver social justice in a meaningful manner. When organized labor help us shape the transition, it is people-centered. And when it is people-centered, the working people will stand in its way and will support it. They will need it. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much, Omar, for bringing the perspective of workers and communities and journalists. And thank you again to all of the panel for your excellent inputs. Thank you. Thank you very much. I think everybody thanked Secretary-General Guterres, and he deserves definitely our thanks because his commitment to this agenda has been absolutely extraordinary. And I was so happy to hear his speech yesterday. and we want to listen to him, continue to listen to him as we go ahead until the choice of a new Secretary General and beyond. And I want to thank Selwyn and the team that has been so wonderful in the preparation of COP30 for organizing this very important opportunity. But what we saw in Belling at COP 30 was a demonstration of resistance. and, in fact, strengthening of multilateralism, because we had an agreement that the United States of America had left, and there was a big concern that we wouldn't be able to have consensus on important issues, that other countries could leave the Paris Agreement. So we saw this symbol of strengthening of multilateralism in Beijing, and I am absolutely sure that under the leadership of my dear friend the Minister from Turkey, my dear Murat, we are going to see the same in Antalya, which will be another demonstration that although we can continue to say multilateralism is in crisis, for climate, we are all united and we want to continue to be together. I think that we have to remember that in Berlin, we also took a very important decision in the Mouchiroun decision, among many important decisions that were mentioned today. We agreed, all of us, by consensus, to have a stronger accent on implementation. It's obvious that the whole world is looking at the negotiations and the negotiations are the essence of COPs. But now we have a mandate from 194 countries to have a much stronger implementation dimension. And this opens extraordinary opportunities, is that under negotiations, we need consensus. And what happened in recent years, the recent COPs have succeeded to close the main negotiations that we committed to do to strengthen Paris and to allow the Paris Agreement to be as effective as possible. So we have the essence of Paris already negotiated so we can implement. What is the difference in the implementation side is that in the implementation side, we don't need consensus. We can have all kinds of coalitions that will pursue the implementation of what we have decided by consensus, all of us countries. And that is why it was very important to see today civil society, to see business, to see subnational governments, these essential actors for the implementation. And we don't need consensus. We can have coalitions that bring extraordinary results. And we can see that in so many dimensions because we heard about methane. We can have coalition. that can reduce, and we know that already, something like 90% of the methane emissions. We have a coalition like the Tropical Forest Forever facility that was launched in Berlin. It's a coalition that is putting together extraordinary resources for conservation of forests that we did not have, and so many other coalitions. So I think that the action agenda is now structured so well because it incorporated the results of the GST. And the Global Stocktake has this advantage. It was a consensus, so we have a mandate, so we can advance in everything that we decided. And we are so excited to see this Action Agenda enriched by the initiatives of Turkey that fit perfectly into the six axes that were presented in Berlin. So I believe that Antalya is going to show how many things we can already do with the decisions we have. It's obvious that we need other decisions and that the negotiations are going to continue to be important, but we have to remember what we can achieve And finally, as was mentioned by some of the speakers, at the end of this year as President of COP, I will present in the first week of November the two roadmaps, one roadmap on fossil fuels and one roadmap on deforestation. Those two roadmaps are based on the mandate that we received in the GST. So they are going to fulfill exactly the wording that we agreed and that we had our consensus in Dubai. And these two roadmaps, I hope, will be well received. And I hope these roadmaps that are an initiative of the Brazilian COP30 presidency, my initiative, but we have to remember this is a mandate that we receive. And I hope it will be an important input for our work preparing the GST2. I think that we cannot forget also that finance is an issue that was raised by basically all the developing countries. And so we are also going to launch a document on implementing the 1.3 trillion of the Bakuto billing that we developed Azerbaijan and Brazil for COP 30, because we heard here developing countries repeated very clearly, it's finance, finance and finance. So I hope that we will keep the spirit of Belen, keep the spirit of Muchido to be able to build with our Turkish presidency a wonderful and splendid and renewed trust in multilateralism, COP, COP 31 in Antalya. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Ambassador, and thank you for your tireless and continued leadership as COP30 President and that of the Government of Brazil. I'll now turn to invite the incoming COP31 President to deliver concluding remarks. Excellency Murak Rum, incoming COP31 President, you have the floor.

Yes, thank you very much, Andre, for what you did and for your remarks. So today we had a very fruitful meeting. So Mr. Secretary General Guterres was here in the beginning. So first of all, I would like to extend my deepest thanks to the government leaders, ministers for coming here, so NGOs being here. I would like to thank each and every one of them for their contributions, for their support to this meeting. Of course, in this process, on one hand, when we are listening to the speakers, the world in an hour, how much emission is emitting, carbon dioxide is emitting? I asked the AI. AI said 6.6 million ton per hour carbon dioxide is being emitted in the world. So during this meeting, approximately in five hours, 33 million tons of carbon dioxide have been emitted. On the 6th of February, 2023, we had an earthquake in our country. And after that earthquake in 11 provinces, the disaster of the century took place. And then under the leadership of our president, His Excellency, Mr. President, we kicked off the rebuilding of the century. And in less than two years, we delivered 455,000 housing units to our people and 23 houses an hour and 550 houses a week. And if you multiply with five, it is like producing 115 houses. So we have seen that energy intensity decreased by 39% in the new building. So they are zero waste compliant and compared to past, they are consuming 39% less energy. They're emitting less carbon dioxide. They're more environmental friendly. They're more livable. So it has such impacts. And now, where will I end up? Because of this, we say implementation. So we have talked enough, we have negotiated, we have made decisions and we have held very important meetings, very important discussions. But now the world is waiting implementation, execution, result, outcome from us. So this bad course, this bad process should be stopped by all of us. The world is waiting for this. And for that reason, we We transferred the flag from Andres, so we transferred their success. So we'll be crowning on to that success and we will be executing their decisions together with our Australian colleagues. And we named our COP implementation COP. And we have our action agenda. We have our objectives target set. And when we have, we will have realized those targets, the emissions in the world, again, will decrease by 20%. when we realize those goals. Six goals. Electrification. So it is 35 by 35 goal for electrification. We will be reducing the increase of waste by half, and we will be increasing the use of circular material by 15%. And energy intensity in buildings, we will be reducing it by 25%. There are six goals. So is it difficult to reach those goals? It's not. So if wanted, anything can be done, we think. Of course, the priorities of Africa and the expectation in Europe may differ, and the need in America and the expectation in Australia, they're all different. We need to evaluate them all together in the same pot. And Everyone's starting point to this process is also different. Think about it. You are born in a country. The conditions of that country cannot be determined by you. But the process following it, the differences, the needs, expectations of that country, by considering all these, we can make progress. We can take steps forward. For a kid in Africa, for a young person in America, or an elderly person in Europe, for all of them, again, we can make this world a livable world. We can show this will all together. This is what we want, with dialogue, consensus, and action. We would like to act. So we would like to listen to anyone, we would like to leave no one behind, we would like to forget nobody. And in this process, we do not want to give up from our speed. And we do not want to compromise justice. Economic structure, development levels of countries, transformation capacities are different. So we need to take steps accordingly. And for that very reason, just in just transition process, rather than one solution or exposing one single solution, we need to have an inclusive and implementable solution which meets the needs of everyone. So here, financial institutions talked and they said, "We are ready." And with Climate Implementation Bridge, those financial institutions in Africa. So we want them to reach those projects of Africa. So we want them to reach fruitful projects by asking AI. I, for example, produced more emissions. AI is also producing emission. Let's use AI, yes, but vis-a-vis climate, we shouldn't turn into a threat. So we need to tidy ourselves up in our lives, in our cities, in our houses. We need to consider, we need to examine all of these and with all these targets and the realization capacity for countries for these goals. Yes, this distance can be fulfilled by finance and technology sharing. and when realizing energy transition, industries, employment, and production and social policies, they have to be taken into consideration comprehensively. Of course, just transition is an obligation where we share burdens, but it should be also seen as a new model of development. Because on one hand, there is development going on. We are writing a new story. So in Strait of Hormuz, in Russia-Ukraine crisis, what we have seen is about our independent security, freedom. So these situations are impacting all these things. For that reason, energy independence of the countries are now national security issues. Every country is dealing with inflation. Why? Because if they invested timely in the past, then if countries were able to produce their energy in their borders, then this crisis wouldn't be this effective today. So women, youth, all workers should be actively involved in this process. This is what we want. And all together, we want to realize this just transition. The discussions of today under all these headings showed us that we need to show this will. We need to demonstrate this will. Every speaker shared their views about this. And we want COP31 a concrete result bearing historical summits rather than where we discuss decisions. And our success in just transition, we will measure it with one single question. So when accelerating transformation, transition by hugging everyone, can we go forward? So Can we handle the needs of everyone? And as COP31 presidency, we to answer this question positively with all parties and with all institutions, we will be, we are ready to work hand in hand. In Antalya, we'll be talking about the importance of just transition, but we will go beyond and under different conditions, how we can realize this. we will be showing a very strong will to this question and we would like to reach an outcome for this. And here I would like to invite all countries to make these decisions in Antalya and to realize this implementation in Antalya. Once again, I would like to extend my gratitude to Mr. Secretary General Selwyn Hart and Andre. Andre is really Andra is giving a great struggle. He is living this. So thank you very much for being here. And I would like to extend my thanks to each and every one of you, dear participants. I would like to express my warmest greetings to all of you. Thank you.
